content: Rh incompatibility is a medical condition that occurs when a pregnant woman has Rh-negative blood, and the fetus she is carrying has Rh-positive blood. This incompatibility can lead to complications during pregnancy and after birth. Symptoms of Rh Incompatibility: Rh incompatibility can present with symptoms that range from mild to severe, potentially life-threatening. In its mildest form, it causes the destruction of red blood cells in the fetus or newborn. After birth, affected infants may exhibit: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes (jaundice). Low muscle tone (hypotonia) and lethargy. Causes of Rh Incompatibility: During pregnancy, fetal red blood cells can cross into the mother’s bloodstream via the placenta. If the mother is Rh-negative, her immune system recognizes the Rh-positive fetal cells as foreign and produces antibodies against them. These anti-Rh antibodies can cross back into the placenta and attack the fetus’s red blood cells, leading to their destruction. The breakdown of red blood cells produces bilirubin, which can cause jaundice in the infant. The bilirubin levels can range from mild to dangerously high. Since it takes time for the mother’s immune system to develop antibodies, firstborn infants are often unaffected unless the mother has been sensitized by previous miscarriages or abortions. Subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies are at higher risk. Diagnosis: Before delivery, the mother may develop an increased amount of amniotic fluid around the fetus (polyhydramnios). Diagnostic findings may include: A positive direct Coombs test result. Elevated bilirubin levels in the baby’s umbilical cord blood. Evidence of red blood cell destruction in the infant’s blood. Treatment Options: Rh incompatibility is preventable with the use of Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM), making prevention the most effective approach. Treatment for an affected infant depends on the severity of the condition: Mild cases may be managed with feeding and hydration. Phototherapy using bilirubin lights may be employed to reduce bilirubin levels. Prevention: Rh incompatibility is almost entirely preventable with proper prenatal care. Rh-negative mothers should be closely monitored by their obstetricians during pregnancy. RhoGAM injections are used to prevent the development of antibodies against Rh-positive blood. These injections are administered: During the second trimester if the father is Rh-positive or if his blood type is unknown. Within a few days after delivery if the baby is Rh-positive. During every pregnancy, after a miscarriage or abortion, following prenatal tests like amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, or after abdominal trauma during pregnancy. When to Seek Medical Care: Contact your healthcare provider if you suspect or confirm pregnancy and have not yet seen a doctor. Prognosis: Full recovery is expected in cases of mild Rh incompatibility. Possible Complications: Severe complications may include: Brain damage due to high bilirubin levels (kernicterus). Fluid accumulation and swelling in the fetus (hydrops fetalis). Long-term issues with mental function, movement, hearing, speech, and seizures.
